holidays.name: National Bad Poetry Day
holidays.description: Today is your license to rhyme 'orange' with something absurd, rhapsodize about your sandwich, and write verse so cringeworthy it circles back to charming. The worse the couplet, the better the celebration. Gather friends for an open-mic of terrible poems, or scribble a limerick that goes nowhere.
holidays.origin: An unofficial observance with no clearly documented founder. It exists as a cheeky counterpoint to more serious poetry celebrations, giving amateur wordsmiths permission to be gloriously awful.
holidays.funFact: Bad poetry has a proud tradition: Scottish poet William McGonagall is widely celebrated as one of the worst poets in the English language, yet he's still beloved and read aloud today for its unintentional comedy.

holidays.name: National Fajita Day
holidays.description: A sizzling salute to the platter that arrives at your table with smoke, sound effects, and a tortilla-wrapped payoff. Grilled strips of marinated meat, peppers, and onions get piled into warm tortillas with all the fixings. Cue the dramatic sizzle.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food observance celebrating the Tex-Mex favorite, which grew out of Texas ranch-hand cooking, where cheaper cuts of beef like skirt steak were grilled over open fires and wrapped in tortillas.
holidays.funFact: The word 'fajita' comes from the Spanish 'faja,' meaning 'belt' or 'girdle,' a nod to the strip-shaped skirt steak that made the dish famous.

holidays.name: National Mail Order Catalog Day
holidays.description: A nostalgic nod to the era of flipping through thick paper catalogs, circling wishlist items, and dreaming of everything from tools to toys delivered right to your door. Dust off a catalog, or browse online for the modern version.
holidays.origin: The day marks August 18, 1872, when Aaron Montgomery Ward produced the first mail order catalog, a single sheet of price listings that launched a retail revolution.
holidays.funFact: Montgomery Ward's first catalog was just one page, but it grew into a massive book, and the company's guarantee of satisfaction or your money back was radical for its time.
